# A guardrails record fits the store, or its check fails

Status: the maintainer ruled, on [issue #605](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/issues/605), that a guardrails record must fit the store's 4 MiB record limit, and that one which cannot fit even with every finding's detail left out fails closed. Trimming the check's own findings, rather than only the exported record, is the builder's choice, which the coordinator agreed on 2026-11-20; it is not a ruling.

The port, `RecordStore`, promises what rule 3 says and no more. `add` checks each record whole. `list` checks envelopes only and leaves payloads to the caller's `RecordSet`, so a record set aside as untrusted cannot stop a listing. Both adapters validate a whole batch before they write any of it, but the port does not require that, since rule 3 lets a batch land in part. The conformance suite asserts only that a refused record never lists and that a repeat of the rest completes the batch. Every adapter refuses a record whose canonical bytes pass `recordLimit`, 4 MiB of UTF-8, with `invalidRecord`, through `SharedRecord.storable()`, and measures the whole batch before it writes any of it; the conformance suite holds every adapter to that, at the limit and a byte past it. The relay takes a file up to the same limit, so the head's job never hands over a record no store keeps. A ruling on the limit changes that one number. A check record's sightings get the limit less `envelopeAllowance`, 4 KiB for the envelope and the check's result, as `SightingBudget.checkRecord`. Problem: a head that changes 1,500 workspace manifests, each naming twenty long scripts, writes a guardrails record of about 5 MB, and the store refuses it. Solution: `fit(findings)` walks the findings in ID order and keeps each one's detail while the full findings so far and the shortest form of every later one fit. Each later finding is `abridged(note)`: What becomes its fixed headline, unless its own What is shorter in UTF-8 bytes, Why here becomes "Melian left out the detail for N more files to keep this record under its limit; `git diff` shows those files.", with N the files those findings name, and its ID, rule, severity, resolution, place, snippet, trigger and What to do stay. A finding that abridging would not make smaller, because its Why here is shorter than the note, keeps its detail, so no finding grows. The same findings give the same bytes. When even every finding abridged does not fit, `fit` throws `RecordError` `recordTooLa [cut at 2 KiB]

The store promises this much and no more:

- `add` can be repeated: the same bytes twice are one record. A batch may land in part, and a repeat completes it.
- `list` is fresh: it returns every record whose `add` returned before the call. A store that can only answer from a stale copy fails the call, and is no record store. The first draft let `list` be stale, and each rule built to survive that, a cell naming the rounds, a watermark for publication, was a new thing to forge.
- `readCell` is fresh: it returns the last value a `writeCell` stored.
- `writeCell` succeeds only when the cell's version is still `expectedVersion`. A version is opaque and changes on every successful write, never a hash of the value, and a writer that dies leaves nothing that blocks the next. The conformance suite holds the case of a value that went away and came back.
- `dispose` first writes a disposal mark to the cell, and `add` refuses a changeset whose cell holds one. Disposal is permanent: the port has no way to recreate a changeset, since one would need an incarnation every record and writer carries.
- It promises no ordering of records, no history, no transaction across records, no secrecy, and no identity for a writer.

The cell holds one small JSON value: the publication lease and the disposal mark. No verdict reads it.

The decision index retires a superseded target whole. A replacement saying “only for X” loses every other clause unless it restates them. Reviewers found such omissions on [pull request #116](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/pull/116) and [pull request #117](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/pull/117).

`Amends: <target link>, <scope>` declares a narrow change to an active target. Effective amendments are only its active Amends sources. The index renders the target as `[ACTIVE; amended by Y]`. The design lens reads the target and its effective amendments; where they conflict, the amendment wins. An amendment alone retires nothing.

If B amends A and C supersedes B, A stays active without B as an amendment. B is history, and the lens receives no conflict authority for it. Two active amendments of one target both stand, including when one also amends the other.

An Amends edge to an inactive target invalidates the graph, even when its source is inactive. Refuse it as a cycle is refused. Name the target, say it is inactive, and name every active successor reachable through Supersedes edges to amend instead. The graph already gives Supersedes precedence when one source declares both edge kinds to the same target; that pair creates no amendment edge. Separate sources amending and superseding one target still leave an invalid amendment target.

`Supersedes:` means whole retirement. Restate every surviving clause in the replacement. Every new or changed edge draws one P3 `guardrail/supersession-drop` notice on the declaring file, even when every clause is restated. The notice says which target is retired and asks the author to restate what survives. Uncarried sentences are evidence, never the trigger. Exact text cannot distinguish a rewrite from a lost obligation.

The port, `RecordStore`, promises what rule 3 says and no more. `add` checks each record whole. `list` checks envelopes only and leaves payloads to the caller's `RecordSet`, so a record set aside as untrusted cannot stop a listing. Both adapters validate a whole batch before they write any of it, but the port does not require that, since rule 3 lets a batch land in part. The conformance suite asserts only that a refused record never lists and that a repeat of the rest completes the batch. The cell holds one JSON value, and `writeCell` refuses any other with `invalidCell`. It sets no size bound: the decision calls a cell small and gives no number, and the build that defines the lease, [issue #396](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/issues/396), sets one. A `writeCell` that fails `unreachable` may have landed, as the git adapter's push stopped at its deadline may, so a repeat with the same expected version can answer `false` for the caller's own write. A caller that repeats one reads the cell, and a cell holding the value it wrote means its write landed. Only a value that names its writer, as a lease's incarnation does, tells the two apart; the publication lease is the first caller. Only `dispose` writes the disposal mark, `{"disposed":true}`, by compare-and-set over whatever the cell held; `writeCell` refuses that value with `invalidCell`. From then on `list` answers nothing, and `add` and `writeCell` throw `RecordError` `disposed`, so a record a dying `add` left after the mark never lists. A version is opaque and never reused: the memory adapter mints a random one on every write and the directory adapter numbers them, so a value that went away and came back never matches a version read before. That holds while only the store touches its own files. Someone who deletes a changeset's `.cell` directory by hand restarts the directory adapter's numbers at 1, so a version read before the deletion can match again. Only a writer with access to the store can do that, and rule 6 trusts such a writer. That [cut at 2 KiB]

explanation.what: This new decision changes the active RecordStore contract without declaring an `Amends:` edge to the shared-record decision, and the implementation also silently strengthens partial `add` into preflight atomicity for an oversized record.
explanation.whatToDo: Declare an `Amends:` edge to `2026-11-13-shared-record-behind-a-store-port.md`, scoped to the record-size and batch-refusal rules, and make the chosen partial-batch semantics explicit. If partial landing remains allowed, assert only that the oversized record never lists; otherwise explicitly amend the base rule before requiring whole-batch preflight.
explanation.whyHere: The active base decision says the port promises its listed semantics “and no more” and explicitly permits a batch to land in part. Because this file is not an effective amendment, the decision index and future design reviews continue to present that old contract while the new conformance case rejects adapters that implement it.

properties.failureScenario: A RecordStore adapter written to active rule 3 streams `add([small, past])`: it stores `small`, then detects that `past` is 4 MiB + 1 byte and rejects it. The base contract explicitly allows that partial landing, but the new conformance case requires `list()` to be empty, so the conforming adapter now fails the suite. Since the added decision has no `Amends:` declaration, its implementer and later reviewers are still given the old partial-batch contract as the active standard.

# A guardrails record fits the store, or its check fails

Status: the maintainer ruled, on [issue #605](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/issues/605), that a guardrails record must fit the store's 4 MiB record limit, and that one which cannot fit even with every finding's detail left out fails closed. Trimming the check's own findings, rather than only the exported record, is the builder's choice, which the coordinator agreed on 2026-11-20; it is not a ruling.

## Problem

Every record store refuses a record past core's `recordLimit`, 4 MiB. A head that changes many workspace manifests makes one guardrails finding per manifest, each naming the scripts it changes, and their record can pass the limit. The store then refused the round's records after the harness had stored a verdict of findings, so the review threw a store error with that verdict standing.

Example: 1,500 changed manifests, each naming twenty long scripts, wrote a guardrails record of about 5 MB.

## Choice

- Past the limit, the guardrails check leaves out the detail of its last findings in ID order, as `SightingBudget.checkRecord.fit` does. A trimmed finding keeps its ID, rule, severity, resolution, place and What to do, so what blocks is unchanged. Its Why here names how many files lost their detail and says that `git diff` shows them. A finding that trimming would not make smaller keeps its detail.
- A record that still passes the limit with every finding trimmed fails the guardrails check, with `RecordError` `recordTooLarge` and a fixed sentence that holds no finding's text. The review reads not reviewed, and its records export.
- The trim applies to the check's own findings, not only to the exported record. The verdict's fingerprint hashes the findings' text, so trimming at export alone would give the local and the shared verdict different texts for one round.

## What it costs
